text: The bay lies quiet under a waning gibbous moon, the water near its warmest for the year, though that warmth arrived a week late by the record and the whole summer has carried that lag forward. Joe-pye weed stands tall in the low ground along the bay shore, its dusky-rose heads just opening where the soil stays wet. Goldenrod has begun to show gold along the roadsides north toward the AuSable country, later than most Augusts allow. Katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the shrub edges. Trico spinners are due on the AuSable in the early morning hours, small and pale above the slow pools. A snowy egret works the shallows. Walleye have dropped to the deep basin. Walk a wet meadow margin at dusk and listen for the first katydid to go quiet.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, its surface the color of old pewter where cloud shadow crosses it. Lake Huron is at or near its annual high, and the warmth that has built since May now peaks in soil and water alike, though seven days behind where the record says it should be. Joe-Pye weed stands tall in the wet margins along the Thumb roads, its dusky-rose heads just opening, a week later than a normal year would show. Goldenrod is breaking into first bloom along those same roadsides. After dark, the first katydids should be audible in the shrubby edges. Whitetail bucks carry their velvet racks into the August browse. Walk any alder run feeding the AuSable before dawn and listen for the thin, rising rasp of katydids beginning their long argument with the night.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, barely a ripple crossing the shallows off Quanicassee, and the water has reached its annual high. Seven days behind the record, August is doing its work slowly. Joe-Pye weed stands head-high in the wet ditches along Rinde Road, its dusky-rose heads just opening where they should have opened the week before. Goldenrod is breaking yellow along the field edges, though a normal year would show it further along by now. At night the katydids have taken up their rasping, the surest sound of summer turning. White-tailed bucks carry full velvet racks in the oak edges north toward the AuSable. Walk any riverside wet meadow at first light and look for trico spinners hovering in slow columns above the current.

The bay lies nearly flat under a full moon that sets just as the trico spinners begin their morning fall above the slower AuSable backwaters. Seven days behind the record, goldenrod has only now opened its first heads along M-55, and joe-pye weed stands in the wet ditches with its dusky-rose crowns just reaching their best. Katydids have taken up their rasping in the oaks after dark, marking the turn more honestly than any calendar. Whitetail bucks carry velvet racks still weeks from hardening. Walleye have dropped to deep cool water in the bay, absent from the shallows. The trico hatch is the thing to watch: be on the river at first light, look for the spinner fall in slow water where riffles ease into pools.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, wind barely enough to crease the surface, and Lake Huron is at or near its annual high-water mark. Seven days behind the record, the season has compressed its milestones: goldenrod is only now opening its first yellow heads along M-25, and joe-pye weed stands in the low wet margins still climbing toward full bloom. Katydids have started their nighttime rasp from the woodlots inland. Trico spinners are due on the AuSable in the early morning hours, spent and falling to the film by mid-morning. Walleye have retreated to deep cool water and will not return to the shallows until autumn stirs the thermocline. Whitetail bucks are still in velvet. Walk the river road at first light and listen for the tricos over the riffles.

The bay lies flat and warm, its surface near the annual high that comes each August to Lake Huron before the long cooling begins. A snowy egret works the shallows somewhere along the Thumb shore, which is about right for this week. Joe-pye weed stands tall in the low ground beside every wet ditch, its dusky-rose heads open now, and goldenrod has started to show its first yellow along the roadsides, though both are arriving a week later than the record expects. Katydids have begun their nighttime rasp in the oaks. Whitetail bucks carry antlers still wrapped in velvet. On the AuSable before first light, trico spinners should be falling to the surface in their brief morning window, worth a look from any accessible riffle.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, its surface warm and unreflective as old pewter. Lake Huron sits at or near its annual high, and the light is already beginning its slow retreat, though summer refuses to acknowledge the fact. Joe-pye weed stands head-high in the low ground along the Sebewaing flats, its dusky-rose heads not yet fully open where they should be, the season running eight days behind and wearing it. Goldenrod is breaking into first bloom along every gravel road through the Thumb. After dark, listen along any brushy field edge for the first katydids, their rasp the one sound that announces August has made up its mind. Whitetail bucks carry new racks still soft under velvet. Walleye have dropped into deep water. In three weeks, the warblers will be moving.

The trico hatch is on the AuSable now, those tiny morning spinners falling to the surface in the early light before the heat sets in, and eight days behind the record means the whole sequence runs compressed and late. Joe-pye weed stands in the low wet ground along the bay shore, its dusky rose heads open and drawing the last of the summer's fritillaries. Katydids have taken over the nights from the crickets. Goldenrod has broken along every field edge and gravel road through the Thumb country. The Blackburnian Warbler appearing here is the first whisper of what is coming within three weeks, when the fall warbler push will fill every woodlot. Stand at the river at first light and watch the trico spinners against the dark water.

The trico hatch is on the AuSable now, those tiny spinners gathering in the morning air above the riffles before the light gets high. With the season running eight days behind, the goldenrod along the Thumb roadsides is only just opening where it should already be well along, and the Joe-pye weed in the low wet ground is the same, its dusky rose heads barely full. Katydids have begun their nighttime work in the shrubs. Walleye have moved off the flats and down into cooler water. The first Blackburnian warblers are moving through, early scouts of the fall flight that is still building. Stand at the river at first light and watch the trico spinners fall.

The trico hatch is underway on the AuSable, those tiny morning spinners gathering above the riffles in the pale light before the sun clears the trees. Eight days behind the long record, the season has held everything back a notch, so goldenrod along the Thumb roadsides and joe-pye weed in the wet swales are blooming later than an old observer would expect. Katydids have begun their nighttime rasp in the willows near the bay margin. A bay-breasted warbler has appeared, an early signal of what is coming: fall warbler movement is three weeks out at most. The walleye are already holding deep and cool. Watch the AuSable riffles at first light for the trico spinner fall, a gauze of wings just above the water.

Eight days behind the record, the goldenrod that should have opened along the Thumb roadsides by the tenth is only now sending up its first yellow heads. Joe-Pye weed stands tall in the low wet margins, its dusky-rose clusters drawing the last of the summer's fritillaries. Katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the woodlines, a sound that belongs to August whatever the calendar delay. Trico spinners fall to the AuSable in the early morning, their spent wings flat on the surface in the brief window after sunup. The bay lies calm and warm, its walleye settled into the deep cool channels. Bay-breasted warblers are moving through, early outriders of the fall flight still three weeks from its peak. Walk the AuSable at first light and watch the flat water for the trico spinner fall.

Nine days behind the record, and goldenrod that should be well along the roadsides is only now showing its first color. Joe-pye weed stands tall in the low ground along the Rifle River corridor, its dusky-rose heads finally opening where the soil stays wet. Katydids have begun their nighttime rasp in the woodlots, the surest low thermometer of late summer. On the AuSable in the early morning hours, trico spinners are due above the riffles, the air briefly thick with those minute flies before the sun climbs. Fall warblers are moving quietly through the shoreline shrubs, their confusing plumage asking more of the eye than spring ever did. The salmon run is still three weeks out, but a late year pushes it later still. Stand at the edge of any wet meadow near the bay at dusk and listen for the katydids.

Nine days behind the record, the summer yet holds its long light over Saginaw Bay, though the light itself is leaving by quiet degrees. Joe-pye weed stands tall in the wet margin ditches along the Thumb roads, its dusky rose heads not yet at full color but close. Goldenrod is opening along every field edge, a little later than the record expects. Trico spinners should be falling in the AuSable mornings now, those tiny mayflies dropping to the surface in the early calm before the heat. Katydids have taken up their night rasping, which is the season's own clock running regardless of the calendar's lag. Walleye have dropped to deep cool water in the bay. Watch the AuSable at first light for the trico spinner fall, where the quiet surface will show the rings of feeding fish.

Nine days behind the record, and the bay feels it. Goldenrod has opened along the roadsides from Standish south to the flats above Bay City, but the heads are sparser and paler than a normal late August warrants. Joe-Pye weed stands tall in the wet ditches beside the Rifle River road, its dusky-rose clusters drawing the last tiger swallowtails of summer. After dark, the katydids rasp from every woodlot, that sound being as reliable a marker of the turning year as any bloom. Trico spinners are on the water in the early morning above the AuSable, small enough to overlook unless the light is right. Warblers are moving through in fresh plumage that gives little away. Walk a weedy field edge at first light and sort the goldenrod visitors by wing.

The goldenrod is opening along the field margins inland from the bay, and joe-pye weed stands tall and dusky-rose in the wet ground at ditch edges, both arriving close to ten days behind where the calendar usually finds them. Nights carry the dry rasp of katydids now, a sound that belongs to the last third of summer. Trico spinners are due on the AuSable each morning, those tiny upwings falling spent on the surface in the early light. Warblers are moving through in the quiet confusing plumage of late August, neither here nor there in their coloring. The salmon run and the first sugar maple color are three weeks out. Walk the AuSable at first light and look low over the water for the trico spinner fall.

Goldenrod has opened along the roadsides and field margins of the Thumb, right on its calendar, though the plants themselves stood green and shut longer than usual this year, the season running ten days behind where it normally stands in late August. Katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the woodlots, and on calm mornings the trico spinners should be falling on the AuSable in the first light, those tiny flies massing and dropping above the slower pools. Walleye have retreated into the deep, cool water of the bay. Fall warblers are moving through in their confusing August plumage, and the willows and dogwoods along any brushy creek edge are worth a slow look now, bird by patient bird.

Goldenrod has opened along the roadsides and field edges, though eleven days behind where the record puts it, so the gold that normally crowds late August is only beginning to show. The katydids are rasping after dark, their dry staccato filling the tree lines from Bay City north toward the AuSable country. Trico spinners should be falling on quiet stretches of river in the early morning hours, the spent adults drifting in mats on the surface film. Snowy egrets are working the shallows of the bay's western margins. Warblers are moving through in confusing fall plumage, easy to overlook. Walleye have pushed into the deeper, cooler basins. A walk along any AuSable riffle at first light, eyes on the water surface, will show whether the trico fall has begun.

The goldenrod is opening along the field edges and roadsides of the Thumb, yellow enough now to read from a moving car, though running nearly two weeks behind its usual date. Soil at sixty-six degrees and days already shy of thirteen and a half hours confirm what the calendar alone cannot: the season is late, and what follows will be late too. Katydids rasp through the dark hours. Trico spinners should be falling on the AuSable in the pale window before sunrise, the flies so small they disappear against the sky. Red-necked phalaropes are moving through, most years unremarked. Walleye have dropped into the deep water of the bay. The velvet on white-tail bucks is still intact, and the salmon have not yet entered the rivers. Walk the river at first light and watch for the trico spinner fall on the slow pools.

Goldenrod has opened along the field edges and roadsides, that first hard gold which marks the pivot of the summer as reliably as anything the calendar can offer. Eleven days behind the record, it arrives late, and the asters and sugar maple color it anticipates are late behind it in turn. Trico spinners should be falling on the AuSable through the early morning hours, tiny and pale over the slow pools, the hatch brief enough to miss if the walk to the river is unhurried. Katydids rasp through the night along the bay shore. Walleye have pulled to the cool depths and will stay there until the first cold rains of September begin to move them. A Red-necked Phalarope is worth watching for along the Thumb shoreline now, spinning in the shallows the way its kind does, picking insects from the surface in tight circles.

Goldenrod has not yet opened along the roadsides south of Tawas, which is where it should be standing gold by now, but the buds are tight and the stems are full-grown, and twelve days of borrowed cold will not hold them much longer. Katydids rasp through the dark from the brushy edges near the river mouths, reliable as any calendar. On the AuSable, trico spinners should be gathering above the slower pools in the first hour of morning light, the adults so small they are best seen against the sky rather than the water. Whitetail bucks are working the velvet off in the cedar edges. The salmon are not yet in the rivers but will be, and the sugar maples are still uniformly green, carrying that delay like a debt the season has not yet settled.

Goldenrod has opened along the field edges and roadsides of the Thumb, right on schedule for the date but not for the year, which is running twelve days behind. The katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the hedgerows, and white-tailed bucks are working the velvet from their antlers on saplings at the wood edges. On the AuSable, trico spinners should be gathering over the riffles in the early morning hours, the hatch so small it is easy to miss against the light. Fall warblers are filtering through in their confusing August plumage, neither the birds of spring nor quite what they will become. The salmon run, the first aster bloom, and the early color in the sugar maples are perhaps three weeks out. Walk the AuSable at first light and look low over the water for the trico spinner fall.

Goldenrod has opened along the roadsides and field edges of the Thumb, right on time by the calendar if not by the feel of the air, which still carries more July than August in it. The season runs twelve days behind, and the goldenrod confirms it: the stands are thinner and less advanced than they should be on the last day of August. Katydids rasp after dark. Velvet is coming off the bucks now, rubbed against saplings in the alder edges and young oaks. The trico hatch is underway on calm mornings along the AuSable, those tiny spinners gathering low over the rifle. A Red-necked Phalarope has appeared on the bay, a bird of open water and long distances, and its presence is worth noting: the salmon run and the first aster bloom are still three weeks off.

The last morning of August arrives twelve days behind itself, and the season carries that debt openly. Goldenrod, which should be peaking along the Thumb roadsides by now, is only coming into first bloom, gold still thin and tentative where it ought to be full. Katydids are rasping in the dark, their timing pulled late with everything else. Out on the bay the water holds its summer calm, walleye already retreated to the cool basin deeps. The trico hatch is underway on the AuSable in the early hours, spinners falling on the riffles before full light. Somewhere offshore a Red-necked Phalarope is working the open water, spinning in its small tight circles. The salmon run and the sugar maple's first color are perhaps three weeks out, perhaps more. Walk the AuSable before dawn and watch the trico spinner fall.

Goldenrod has opened along the roadsides east of Bay City, twelve days behind its own average, which means the asters are trailing it at the same interval. The katydids are rasping in the dark nonetheless, indifferent to the calendar's arithmetic. Trico spinners should be falling on the AuSable in the first hour of morning light, the flies so small they look like drifting smoke above the rifle. King salmon are pressing up from the lake into the lower river now, heavy fish running on instinct older than any late season. A waxing gibbous moon will light the riverbanks tonight. Walk the edge of any uncut field at dusk and listen for the first katydid to stop: in the silence that follows, the summer announces what it has left.

The season runs twelve days behind its own record, and what should feel like deep September still carries the thick weight of mid-August. Goldenrod is opening along the roadsides off M-25, later than the old dates suggest it ought to be, and the asters are just beginning their purple along the field margins. Katydids rasp after dark. On the AuSable, trico spinners should be falling in the early morning hours, those tiny spent flies that drift in clusters on the slower flats. King salmon are pushing up from the lake into the lower river now, heavy fish carrying the cold with them. A red-necked phalarope was reported on the bay, a bird worth watching for along the open water, spinning and picking in that restless, particular way it has.

Goldenrod is opening along the roadsides south of Tawas City, and the asters are beginning to show purple at the field edges, though both are running nearly two weeks behind where they stand in an ordinary September. The Trico spinners are on the water in the early morning hours, those tiny flies whose fall to the surface is easy to miss unless you are standing in the river at first light looking upstream. Katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the shrub edges. The king salmon are due in the AuSable now, feeling the pull of the river out of the cold lake. Stand on the Foote Dam access before dawn and watch the holding water for the first dark shapes moving against the current.
